text: Weekly China recap. SMIC reports earnings, Trump/Xi meet next week + $BABA $TCEHY earnings - Big sell-off in offshore China MXCN -4.6% this week while onshore CSI 300 -0.9% - Bessent and Greer held virtual meeting with China Vice Premier He Lifeng on trade/economy. Chinese side expressed serious concerns over recent US actions, probably the MATCH Act (will cross serious redline for China) and RASA https://english.news.cn/20261107/cc78417d6e8640c0b418661eda62f79c/c.html - US/China agreed to extend tariff pause for another 2 months (probably for the last potential Trump/Xi meeting for G20 in Miami in Dec) - Chinese hyperscalers cut enterprise SSD orders due to AI chip supply constraints https://zdnet.co.kr/view/?no=20261112144609 - SMIC reported 3Q'26 earnings, beats across the board, but CapEx is tracking below their 2026 target ($4.5B spent YTD vs. $8.1B target or ~$6.1B by 3Q). Biggest beat was gross margins (~30% vs. consensus at ~26%), but SMIC guides 4Q'26 GM of 27% (midpoint). Revenue guide for 4Q'26 $3,349.5mm (midpoint) vs. ~$3.2B consensus. Still light vs. $TSM TSMC's GM of ~65%. SMIC's operating margins came in at 22.3%, beat vs. consensus, but if TSMC is the ceiling they're far off (~59%) - SMIC stock trades up to as high as +7.3% after posting earnings but ends up flat - MSCI announces quarterly index review results, effective Nov 30 https://www.msci.com/indexes/index-resources/index-review - PPI comes in +5.7% yoy vs. CPI -0.7% yoy in Oct. - Exports +35.2% yoy, with upside surprise in imports of +41.6% (energy driven) - Oct. credit data misses expectations as bank loans contracted. New RMB loans -100B in Oct (vs. +80B consensus). M2 growth 7.1% yoy (vs. 7.2% consensus)

Trump/Xi meeting next week (11/18-11/19) for APEC in China. Good chance they meet again before the year's up in Miami in Dec for G20 Historical performance of US/China stock indexes & select China stocks pre/post their meetings below. Offshore/US-listed China stocks big underperformance so far leading up to the meeting vs. historical averages while onshore mixed. Jensen's affairs are the headline, but the core reason for his ouster is "they" want everything, including AI, to move to the "you will own nothing and be happy" subscription-based, surveillance economy where only large, politically connected firms dominate. Jensen was one the strongest advocates for at least giving us the option to opt out of this arrangement with open source models and having access to competitive compute. A noble mission, but politically naive. Bamboo ceiling also may have played a part and he was never offered a seat at the table Everything else is a sideshow. Jensen wasn’t the first, and he won’t be the last.
